opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important distinctions, and people often blur the two together when they talk about "agents getting better."

For a reliability-type task, what matters is the lower bound. Think customer service, filling out forms, booking a flight, processing a refund. The task itself isn't that hard, and a human can usually do it. But if you deploy it at scale and it fails one time in twenty, that's unacceptable. So the metric you care about is something like "does it succeed every single time," not "can it succeed once." That's partly why, in work like τ-bench, we looked at pass^k, the probability of succeeding on all k trials, rather than pass@k. A model can look great on pass@1 and still fall apart when you ask whether it's consistent across eight tries.

For creativity-type tasks it's almost the opposite. You care about the upper bound. Proving a new theorem, finding a new drug candidate, writing a really good piece of code nobody has written before: if you try a hundred times and one attempt is brilliant, that's enormously valuable, because you can verify it and keep it. There, pass@k is the right mental model, and diversity and exploration matter more than consistency.

The two pull the training and the product design in different directions. For reliability, you want the model to be robust, to follow rules, to handle long-tail user behavior, to ask for clarification instead of guessing. The interaction with humans matters a lot, because real users are messy. For creativity, you want the model to explore, try unusual ideas, and you need a good verifier or environment so you can search over many attempts.

So when someone asks "what's the next big agent application," I think you first have to ask which regime you're in. Many economically valuable tasks today are reliability tasks. They aren't intellectually the hardest, but they're where the gap between a demo and a real product is huge. The frontier research excitement is often about creativity, solving things humans can't. Both matter, but the evaluation, the utility, and even the business model look quite different depending on which one you're targeting.

r001.rationale: It says reliability tasks require succeeding consistently across repeated trials, describing failure one time in twenty as unacceptable and emphasizing success on all k trials.

r002.rationale: It says that for creative tasks, one brilliant attempt among a hundred can be enormously valuable, and frames this as pass@k.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to put it is: reliability is about the variance, and creativity is about the ceiling.

For a reliability task, there's a known correct answer, or at least a known correct behavior, and what you care about is the probability of getting it right every single time. Booking a flight, filling out a form, running a database migration, answering a customer's question about a refund policy. Nobody wants a creative flight booking. If the agent does it right 95% of the time, that's actually a bad agent, because the 5% is what everyone remembers, and the 5% is what breaks trust. So the metric there is something like pass^k rather than pass@k — I want all k attempts to succeed, not just one of them.

For a creativity task, it's the opposite. Writing a proof, finding a new approach to a research problem, coming up with a product idea. There you actually want variance. You want the model to sample broadly, because the value is in the best attempt, not the average one. If an agent tries ten different directions and nine are garbage but one is brilliant, that's a great outcome. Pass@k is the right frame, and k can be large.

What makes this interesting for agents specifically is that most real tasks are a mix, and the mix changes over the course of a single episode. Think about a coding agent. Figuring out the architecture of a fix is a creative step — you want exploration. But once you've committed to an approach, actually editing the files, running the tests, not deleting the wrong directory — that's pure reliability. So the agent has to know which mode it's in. A lot of agent failures I see are a mode confusion: being "creative" during the execution phase, like inventing an API that doesn't exist, or being overly conservative during the exploration phase and just picking the first thing that looks plausible.

The other distinction I'd draw is about the environment. Reliability tasks usually have a verifier that's cheap — the test passes, the form submitted, the number matches. Creativity tasks usually have a verifier that's expensive or doesn't exist, and a human has to judge. That has a big consequence for training. For reliability you can do a lot of RL with dense reward and basically grind the variance down. For creativity, the reward is sparse and noisy, and if you optimize too hard against a weak verifier, you get mode collapse — the model finds one thing the verifier likes and stops exploring. So ironically, over-optimizing for reliability can kill creativity, and I think that's a real tension in how people are training agents right now.

So when I look at a task, I ask two questions: what's the cost of a failure, and what's the value of an outlier success? High cost of failure, low value of outlier — reliability. Low cost of failure, high value of outlier — creativity. And then the hard engineering problem is building an agent that can tell the difference on its own, inside the task, rather than having a human label every step for it.

r001.rationale: The response says reliability means getting the known correct behavior right every time, calls 95% success inadequate, and frames the goal as all k attempts succeeding.

r002.rationale: The response says creativity values the best attempt and gives the example of one brilliant result among ten attempts as a successful outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is how you evaluate success. For some tasks, you know what the correct outcome should look like, and you want the agent to reach it consistently. If I ask an agent to book a flight, it needs to get the date and destination right and respect my budget. A creative interpretation of those constraints is probably a failure.

For other tasks, like brainstorming a research direction, you don’t know the best answer in advance. You want the agent to explore possibilities, including ideas that might not work. If every suggestion is safe and predictable, the agent can be reliable in a narrow sense but still not very useful.

But I wouldn’t divide all tasks into two separate categories. Often, you need creativity during exploration and reliability during execution. In coding, for example, you might explore several approaches to a problem, but the implementation still needs to satisfy the requirements. So the question is: where is variation valuable, and where is it costly? That should shape how much freedom we give the agent and how we verify its work.

r001.rationale: It says reliability-oriented tasks require the agent to reach a known correct outcome consistently, illustrated by getting flight details and budget right.

r002.rationale: It describes exploring possibilities and tolerating ideas that may not work, but does not say that one exceptional result among many attempts can count as success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: how many acceptable outcomes are there, and what happens if the agent gets it wrong? If you’re booking a flight or updating a database, there may be many steps, but the constraints are quite clear. You want the agent to satisfy those constraints consistently. A surprising action is usually a problem.

If you’re brainstorming a research direction or drafting a story, there are many possible good answers. There, you want exploration. An agent that always produces the same safe answer might be reliable in one sense, but it isn’t very useful.

These aren’t completely separate categories, though. A research agent can be creative in proposing hypotheses, but it needs to be reliable when reporting what an experiment actually showed. So I would distinguish them at the level of individual steps: where should the agent explore, and where should it verify? The challenge is giving it freedom where variation creates value, while making sure that freedom doesn’t turn into unsupported claims or unintended actions.

r001.rationale: The response says constraint-based tasks should be handled consistently, but does not clearly require near-error-free performance across repeated instances.

r002.rationale: The response values exploration and recognizes many possible good answers, but does not say that one exceptional result across many attempts can count as success.
